entry: Keyboard layout for Latin-script alphabets, named for the first six keys of its top letter row. It evolved for quick typing of English on [[Typewriter|typewriters]] and is based on a layout included on the Sholes and Glidden typewriter, sold by E. Remington and Sons from 1874. Its popularity grew after the Remington No. 2 of 1878. Christopher Latham Sholes, a [[Newspaper|newspaper]] editor who lived in Kenosha, [[Wisconsin]], filed a [[Patent|patent]] for his early machine in 1867. QWERTY remains a de facto standard on computers, and Dvorak and Colemak are prominent alternatives.

Underground water supply system developed in ancient [[Iran]], which carries water to the surface from an [[Aquifer|aquifer]] or well through a buried [[Aqueduct (water supply)|aqueduct]]. Originating about 3,000 years ago, it is known by regional names including kārēz in Afghanistan and Pakistan, foggāra in Algeria and khettāra in the Atlas Mountains. A typical qanat is a gently sloping tunnel reached through well-like vertical shafts. Gravity delivers the water to the surface at a lower point, so no pumping is needed. Because the water travels underground, little is lost to [[Evaporation|evaporation]]. The system also resists floods and earthquakes and is almost insensitive to variations in rainfall. Qanats still supply water for drinking and irrigation in hot, arid regions, and the largest working examples are in Afghanistan, [[Xinjiang]], [[Oman]] and Pakistan.

Flag carrier airline of [[Australia]], and the largest airline in Oceania by fleet size, international flights and international destinations. One of the world's oldest airlines still in operation, it was founded in November 1920 as Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Services; Qantas is an acronym of that name. It is based in Mascot, [[Sydney]], beside its main hub at Sydney Airport. It is the only airline in the world that flies to all seven continents. As of March 2023, the Qantas Group held a 60.8% share of the Australian domestic market.

Persianate, Muslim Turkoman dynasty, also called the Black Sheep Turkomans. It ruled a territory comprising present-day [[Azerbaijan]], Armenia, northwestern [[Iran]], eastern Turkey and northeastern Iraq from about 1374 to 1468. Its name likely refers to the black sheep painted on its flags. The dynasty was initially a vassal of the Jalayirid Sultanate. In 1400 the [[Timurid Empire]] under [[Timur]] defeated it, and its leader Qara Yusuf fled to the [[Mamluk Sultanate]] in Egypt. Qara Yusuf later regained power, and [[Baghdad]] was captured in 1410. The dynasty's decline followed conflict with the rival [[Aq Qoyunlu]], which absorbed its territories by 1469.

Country in [[West Asia]] that occupies a peninsula on the northeastern coast of the [[Arabian Peninsula]]. Its sole land border is with [[Saudi Arabia]], and the rest of its territory is surrounded by the [[Persian Gulf]]. Most of the land is flat, low-lying desert, and the capital, [[Doha]], is home to over 80% of the inhabitants. The House of Thani has ruled Qatar as a hereditary monarchy since an 1868 agreement with Britain. It became a British protectorate in 1916 and gained independence in 1971. Under the constitution, the emir holds nearly all executive, legislative and judicial authority and appoints the prime minister and cabinet. The economy is built on its [[Natural gas|natural gas]] reserves, and Qatar is one of the world's largest exporters of liquefied natural gas.

Iranian island in the [[Strait of Hormuz]], the largest island in the [[Persian Gulf]]. It covers 1,491 sq km and is 135 km long. It lies a few km off the southern Iranian coast, separated from the mainland by the Clarence Strait. The island holds the Namakdan [[Salt]] Cave, at 6.6 km long one of the longest known salt caves in the world, where salt and sulphur were traditionally mined. The cave forms the key geosite of the Qeshm Island UNESCO Global Geopark.

Vital force in [[Chinese philosophy]] and traditional medicine, traditionally believed to be part of all living things. Literally meaning "vapor", "air", "gas" or "breath", the word *qi* is often translated as "vital energy" or simply "energy". It is a concept in [[Traditional Chinese medicine]] and [[Chinese martial arts]], where attempts to cultivate and balance qi are called qigong. Believers hold that good health requires its unimpeded flow, and [[Acupuncture|acupuncture]] is one practice said to affect it. Originally prescientific, the idea is today considered pseudoscientific, because it does not correspond to the concept of energy used in the physical sciences.

Fifth emperor of the [[Qing dynasty]] of China (r. 1735–1796). The fourth and favorite son of the Yongzheng Emperor, he was an ambitious military leader. His campaigns reached Inner Asia, Burma, [[Nepal]] and [[Vietnam]], and he conquered [[Xinjiang]] from the [[Dzungar Khanate]], ordering the Dzungar genocide. As a patron of the arts, he sponsored the *Siku Quanshu* (Complete Library of the Four Treasuries), and literary inquisitions in his reign suppressed some 3,100 works. In 1796 he abdicated after a 60-year reign, leaving his grandfather, the [[Kangxi Emperor]], as the longest-reigning Qing emperor, but he continued to rule as Emperor Emeritus until his death. He ruled at the end of the High Qing era, when military weakness, corruption and stagnation followed.

First imperial dynasty of China, named for the state of Qin, a fief of the [[Zhou dynasty]]. Qin conquered the rival states of the [[Warring States period]] from 230 BC and unified China in 221 BC. Its king, Ying Zheng, took the title [[Qin Shi Huang]], or first emperor of China. Reforms by [[Shang Yang]] strengthened the state, and under Qin the currency, weights, measures and [[Writing system|writing system]] were standardized. The dynasty built the walls that became the [[Great Wall of China]], a national road system and the mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang, guarded by the [[Terracotta Army]]. Lasting only 14 years, with two emperors, it was the shortest of any major Chinese dynasty. It collapsed in revolt after Qin Shi Huang's death, and the [[Han dynasty]] that followed kept many of its administrative practices.

Manchu-led imperial dynasty of China, the last in Chinese history, which ruled from 1644 to 1912. It grew from the Later Jin state founded by [[Nurhaci]] in 1616, and his son [[Hong Taiji]] proclaimed the Great Qing in 1636. Qing forces seized [[Beijing]] from the [[Ming dynasty]] in 1644. At its height the empire stretched from the Sea of Japan to the Pamir Mountains, and under the [[Qianlong Emperor]] it assembled the territorial base of modern China. The [[Taiping Rebellion]] and the Dungan Revolt caused the deaths of over 20 million people. Defeat in the [[First Sino-Japanese War]] (1894–1895) cost China its influence over Korea and led to the cession of Taiwan to the [[Empire of Japan]]. Reforms after 1900 included elections, a new legal code and the abolition of the imperial examination system, but Manchu conservatives later blocked them. The Wuchang Uprising of October 10, 1911 led to the Xinhai Revolution, and the abdication of the Xuantong Emperor on February 12, 1912 ended the dynasty.

Prefecture-level city in [[Shandong]] province, China, lying across the Shandong Peninsula on the [[Yellow Sea]]. It is a major seaport, naval base and commercial center, and a key city of the [[Belt and Road Initiative]]. The 2020 census recorded 7,172,451 people in its built-up area of seven urban districts. [[Germany]] acquired the city in 1897 as a base for its East Asia Squadron, and [[Japan]] occupied it in 1914 during [[World War I]]. Shandong reverted to Chinese control in 1922 after [[United States|American]] mediation at the Washington Naval Conference. Qingdao's German-style architecture and the Tsingtao Brewery, China's second largest brewery, are legacies of the German period.

Largest lake in China, an alkaline [[Endorheic basin|endorheic]] salt lake in Qinghai Province, to which it gave its name. It lies about 100 kilometers west of Xining, at 3,205 meters above sea level in a hollow of the [[Tibetan Plateau]]. The lake shrank over much of the 20th century but has grown since 2004. It had a surface area of 4,317 square kilometers and an average depth of 21 meters, with a maximum depth of 25.5 meters in 2008. Its water is saline, at about 1.4% salt by weight, and alkaline, with a pH of 9.3. The lake was isolated from the [[Yellow River]] about 150,000 years ago. Known in English as Koko Nor, its name is often translated as "Blue Sea" or "Green Sea".

Capital of Qom Province in central [[Iran]], about 140 km south of [[Tehran]] on the Qom River. It is a holy city of [[Shia Islam]], the site of the Fatima Masumeh Shrine, a descendant of the Islamic prophet [[Muhammad]]. Qom is the world's largest center for Shia Islamic scholarship, and its economy depends heavily on pilgrimage, with around 20 million visiting each year. Jamkaran Mosque, another Shia holy site, draws millions each year to celebrate Mid-Sha'ban. Qom is also an industrial center and a regional hub for the distribution of [[Petroleum|petroleum]] products. Imam Khomeini International Airport, the largest airport in Iran, lies between Qom and Tehran.

Chinese poet and statesman of the state of Chu during the [[Warring States period]]. He served as Left Minister under King Huai of Chu until corrupt ministers slandered him, and he was later exiled to the regions south of the [[Yangtze]]. The main source on his life is the biography by [[Sima Qian]] in the *Records of the Grand Historian*, which contains contradictory details. He is the central figure of the *Chu Ci* anthology, and *Li Sao* is generally accepted as his work. He is credited with originating the *sao* style of verse, which used lines of varying length rather than four-character lines. He is regarded as one of the most prominent figures of [[Romanticism]] in Chinese classical literature. Later tradition says he drowned himself in the Miluo River, a story linked to the Dragon Boat Festival.

Promotion of fraudulent or ignorant medical practices, often synonymous with health fraud. The term comes from the Dutch *kwakzalver*, a "hawker of salve", and quacksalvers sold their ointments at markets by shouting to attract buyers. Common features include questionable diagnoses and untested or refuted treatments, especially for serious diseases such as cancer. Many remedies contained no effective ingredients, though some contained [[Opium|opium]] or [[Alcohol (drug)|alcohol]] that gave symptomatic relief. Some ingredients had real effects: [[Willow|willow]] bark contains [[Salicylic acid]], related to [[Aspirin]], and [[Quinine|quinine]] treated [[Malaria]]. Psychiatrist Stephen Barrett defines quackery as the promotion of unsubstantiated methods that lack a scientifically plausible rationale. Courts have ruled that calling someone a quack is not the same as accusing them of fraud.

Second-degree polynomial equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. The name comes from the Latin *quadratus*, "square". The values of x that satisfy it are called roots or zeros. With [[Real number|real]] coefficients, it has two distinct real roots, one repeated real root, or two complex conjugate roots. Solutions can be found by factoring, by completing the square, or with the [[Quadratic formula]], x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a. The discriminant, b² − 4ac, determines which case applies. Problems of this kind were solved as early as 2000 BC, and the graph of a quadratic function is a [[Parabola|parabola]] whose x-intercepts are its roots.

Closed-form expression for the solutions of a quadratic equation in elementary algebra. For coefficients a, b and c, with a ≠ 0, the roots are x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac))/2a, where the ± sign gives two roots. The quantity Δ = b² − 4ac is the discriminant: if it is positive, the roots are two distinct real numbers; if zero, one repeated real root; and if negative, two complex conjugate roots. Geometrically, the roots are the points where the [[Parabola|parabola]] crosses the x-axis. Completing the square yields the same solutions.

Four-sided [[Polygon|polygon]], having four edges and four vertices, also called a tetragon. The interior angles of a simple planar quadrilateral add up to 360 [[Degree (angle)|degrees]]. Simple quadrilaterals are either convex, with all interior angles less than 180 degrees, or concave; self-intersecting quadrilaterals are called complex. Special convex types include the [[Trapezoid|trapezoid]], with at least one pair of parallel sides; the parallelogram, with two pairs; the [[Rhombus|rhombus]], with four equal sides; the rectangle, with four [[Right angle|right angles]]; and the [[Square]], which is both a rhombus and a rectangle. Kites have two pairs of adjacent equal sides. All non-self-crossing quadrilaterals tile the plane.

Members of the Religious Society of Friends, a historically Protestant Christian movement. It arose in mid-17th-century England, breaking with the established [[Church of England]]. Friends believe that each person can be guided by an "inward light", and they avoid [[Creed|creeds]] and hierarchical structures. Quakers refused to swear oaths or take part in war, and opposed slavery.Some Quakers founded banks, including Barclays and Lloyds, and confectionery firms such as [[Cadbury]]. Quaker organizations in Britain and the United States shared the 1947 Nobel Peace Prize. In 2017 an estimated 377,557 adult Quakers were counted, 49% of them in Africa.

American technology company headquartered in [[San Diego]], California. Founded on July 1, 1985, by Irwin Jacobs and six other former Linkabit employees, it developed code-division multiple access (CDMA) wireless technology, which was later adopted as a 2G standard in North America. The company holds essential patents for 5G, 4G and other mobile standards, and it designs Snapdragon processors used in many smartphones. It is expanding into [[Internet of things|Internet of Things]] devices, [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] chips and automotive systems. Qualcomm has faced antitrust cases in the [[European Union]], the United States and Asia.

Form of research that gathers and analyzes non-numerical, descriptive data to understand people's [[Social reality|social reality]], including their attitudes, beliefs and motivations. It typically uses in-depth interviews, focus groups or field observation to collect data rich in detail and context. Methods include [[Ethnography|ethnography]], grounded theory, discourse analysis and interpretative phenomenological analysis. Its approaches draw on philosophies including [[Positivism|positivism]], postpositivism, critical theory and constructivism. It is used in [[Sociology]], [[Anthropology]], [[Political science]], [[Psychology]] and software engineering research. Unlike quantitative research, which tests theory with numerical data and seeks generalization, it explores particular cases and the meanings people attach to their experiences. Critics argue that reliance on researcher interpretation risks bias.

Second emperor of the Tây Sơn dynasty of Vietnam (r. 1788–92). Born Nguyễn Huệ, he was one of the three Tây Sơn brothers whose rebellion overthrew the [[Lê dynasty|Later Lê dynasty]] and the rival Nguyễn and Trịnh lords. Regarded as one of Vietnam's most successful military commanders, he defeated a [[Qing dynasty|Qing]] invasion force of over 200,000 troops at the Battle of Ngọc Hồi–Đống Đa in January 1789. He also introduced tax exemptions and promoted the Nôm script for Vietnamese writing. His death marked the start of the dynasty's decline. Nguyễn Ánh overthrew the Tây Sơn and established the [[Nguyễn dynasty]] in 1802.

Research strategy that focuses on quantifying the collection and analysis of data. It is a deductive approach that emphasizes testing theory, shaped by empiricist and [[Positivism|positivist]] philosophies. It is associated with the [[Scientific method|scientific method]], and its work includes generating models, hypotheses and measurement instruments, controlling variables and analyzing empirical data. Quantitative data are numerical, such as statistics or percentages, and researchers hope the analysis will yield results that generalize to a larger population. It is widely used in [[Psychology]], [[Economics]], [[Sociology]] and [[Political science]]. In contrast, [[Qualitative research|qualitative research]] explores meaning in particular experiences. A study of 1,274 articles in the top two American sociology journals, published between 1935 and 2005, found that roughly two-thirds used quantitative methods.

Minimum amount of any physical property involved in an interaction. A quantized property can take only discrete values, which are integer multiples of one quantum (plural quanta). A [[Photon|photon]] is a single quantum of light, and the energy of an [[Electron|electron]] bound within an [[Atom|atom]] is quantized, which keeps matter stable. The modern concept originates with [[Max Planck]]'s report of December 14, 1900, on blackbody radiation. In 1905 [[Albert Einstein]] proposed that light travels in localized packets, which he called quanta of light. Quantization is one of the foundations of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]].

Branch of physical chemistry that applies [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] to chemical systems to predict the physical and chemical properties of molecules and materials. It often involves calculating electronic wave functions, typically by solving the [[Schrödinger equation|Schrödinger equation]] computationally, and uses approximations such as the Born–Oppenheimer approximation to make simulations feasible. Methods include density functional theory, Hartree–Fock calculations, quantum Monte Carlo and coupled cluster methods. In 1916 [[Gilbert N. Lewis]] developed the first working model of valence electrons, and a 1927 article on the [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] molecule by Walter Heitler and Fritz London is often recognized as the field's first milestone. Linus Pauling later integrated this work into [[Valence bond theory|valence bond theory]] in the 1930s.
